newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico's central bank chief defends policies.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico's central bank chief defends policies.

text.p: Banco de Mexico governor Miguel Mancera on Wednesday defended his bank's beleaguered monetary policy, dismissing suggestions that it was creating an imminent inflation threat.

The central bank came under pressure after news reports suggested that a greater-than-expected increase in coins and bills in circulation -- the monetary base -- during May could not be justified by economic conditions and might be inflationary.
But in a rare on-the-record meeting with journalists, Mancera said the bank was only meeting demand for more money and was ready to keep the monetary base above expectations for as long as necessary.

"It all depends if this demand translates into inflationary pressures. If it doesn't produce inflationary pressures, it can continue. If it does produce inflationary pressures, then the central bank will have to act...," Mancera said.
He suggested that a greater worry for the central bank would be to create disinflationary pressures in Mexico's already weakened economy.
Mancera said an increasing demand for money due to economic growth would not be a cause for concern.
"That would not be worrying, and meeting this larger demand for cash is not inflationary. But not meeting this demand for cash could create unnecessary disinflationary pressures," he said.
At the start of the year, the central bank took the unprecedented step of publishing figures for the expected monetary base for each day of the year.
The move to greater openness has exposed the bank to criticism, with economists demanding to know why the base was recently higher than forecast.
Mancera cited several factors including faster-than-expected economic growth in the first quarter and lower interest rates.

Mancera was asked how demand for cash could be strong when numbers like retail sales, released on Wednesday, showed a 3.5 percent decline during the first quarter compared to the same period last year and indicated still weak domestic demand.
He said rising employment and an increase in the informal economy were two factors increasing cash demand.

"The increase in employment produces a large increase in the demand for cash, because a person who doesn't have a job yesterday doesn't have any money in their pocket, but someone who has a job today has money in their pocket," he said.
Mexico also has a flourishing underground economy.
"Registered sales for formal trade could have been affected by sales of informal goods," he said.
The central bank also says that a large number of holidays in the first part of the year caused people to spend more cash instead of spending time earning it.
Another factor was the upcoming elections, as political parties increased campaign spending before the key July 6 votes for the federal Congress and in various states.
